Where tradition-specific distinctives were findable, I have noted them; where I could not reach a source (especially LCMS, Wesleyan/Seedbed, Catholic, and Orthodox pages), I have noted the gap.

## Job 3: Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v.1 — “After this, Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth.”

**Traditional reading:** This marks Job’s first speech after seven days of silent suffering with his three friends. The phrase “opened his mouth” is a Hebrew idiom used on solemn occasions, implying deep, long-repressed thoughts now given expression (Pulpit Commentary). Job cursed his *day*—not God, not his fellow creatures, not himself. Satan had wagered that Job would curse God to His face (Job 1:11; 2:5), but Job never does. Gill notes that the Hebrew word for “cursed” also carries the sense of making light of, despising, or disesteeming the day—wishing it either had never been or be buried in oblivion. God later rebukes Job and Job repents (Job 40:4), so this is not held up as blameless speech, but it is not the blasphemy Satan sought.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-3/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.2 — “And this is what he said:”

Gill notes that the Hebrew literally reads “and Job answered and said,” though nothing had been spoken to him—he “answered” his own calamity and his friends’ silence. This marks the start of the poetic portion of the book (through Job 42:6). The Pulpit Commentary also notes the formula as indicating solemn, deliberate discourse.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.3 — “May the day of my birth perish, and the night it was said, ‘A boy is conceived.’”

**Traditional reading:** Job curses both the day of his birth and the night of his conception. The “night” is personified as speaking the joyful announcement. Gill and the Pulpit Commentary note that a male child was considered a special blessing in the ancient world. Job wishes either that the day had never existed or that its annual return would never be celebrated (his children’s birthdays had been feast days, Job 1:4). Gill also notes that some Jewish writers wrongly inferred from this that Job denied providence and believed in astrological fate; Gill rejects that, citing Job 23:14 which shows Job ascribed all events to God’s purpose.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.4 — “If only that day had turned to darkness! May God above disregard it; may no light shine upon it.”

**Traditional reading:** Job wishes that the day of his birth be plunged into utter darkness—the reverse of Genesis 1:3 (“Let there be light”). As David Guzik (Enduring Word) puts it: “As God had said in Genesis 1:3, ‘Let there be light,’ so Job, using the same terminology, said, ‘As for that day, let there be darkness.’” Ellicott explains “regard” (or “seek”) as: “Let not God stoop from His bright throne to raise it up from its dark hiding-place”—i.e., let God not care for it or providentially bless it (as in Deuteronomy 11:12, where the same verb is used of God’s care for the land). The Pulpit Commentary says Job recognizes that a day cannot literally perish, so he limits himself to wishing darkness and ill omen upon it.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-3/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/3.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/3.htm

---

### v.5 — “May darkness and gloom reclaim it, and a cloud settle over it; may the blackness of the day overwhelm it.”

**Traditional reading:** Ellicott notes that the Hebrew word translated “stain” (BSB “reclaim”) is literally “redeem”—i.e., let darkness and the shadow of death claim that day as their rightful inheritance. The “blackness of the day” is understood by the Pulpit Commentary as the stifling darkness of the *khamsin* (sirocco) wind, which can turn day to night with thick, lurid, oppressive darkness. Gill says the “shadow of death” denotes the deepest darkness, and that Job wishes a thick cloud to dwell permanently on that day.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/3.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.6 — “If only darkness had taken that night away! May it not appear among the days of the year; may it never be entered in any of the months.”

**Traditional reading:** Job now turns to the night of his conception (not birth). Ellicott says the verb is better rendered “let it not rejoice among” the days—personifying the night as excluded from the joyful procession of nights. Gill and the Pulpit Commentary note that the Massoretic pointing supports “rejoice,” but many older translators (LXX, KJV) read “be joined.” Either way, the sense is: let that night be struck from the calendar, never to be counted among the months.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/3.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.7 — “Behold, may that night be barren; may no joyful voice come into it.”

**Traditional reading:** “Barren” (or “solitary,” “sterile”) is interpreted by Gill and the Pulpit Commentary as: let no child be born on that night, and therefore let there be no joyful cry announcing a birth—especially not the joyful shout of “a man-child is conceived” (v.3). The Targum even extends it to no cock-crowing being heard.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.8 — “May it be cursed by those who curse the day—those prepared to rouse Leviathan.”

**Traditional reading:** This is one of the most debated verses in the chapter. Several interpretations appear in the sources:

- **Ellicott:** Let those who proclaim days unlucky or accursed (sorcerers, professional cursers) curse that day as pre-eminently accursed. “Those prepared to rouse Leviathan” are “persons as mad and desperate as that”—those reckless enough to stir up a crocodile. Let the most hopeless and reckless select that day as the one to curse.
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Two views: (a) Let desperate men who curse their own day curse Job’s day too; or (b) Let sorcerers who claim power to curse days and stir up the chaos-dragon Leviathan curse this night. The Pulpit leans toward the second, seeing Job as believing (or speaking as if he believed) in sorcerers’ power.
- **Gill:** Those who are “ready to raise up mourning” (KJV)—professional mourners at funerals who curse the day of a person’s death; or fishermen who, when unsuccessful and in danger from the whale (Leviathan), curse the day.
- **Enduring Word (Guzik, Pentecostal/charismatic):** Job summons ancient soothsayers to curse his birthday—not because he believed in their power, but as vivid communication. Guzik notes that Leviathan (meaning “twisting one”) is a chaos-dragon figure, associated in some rabbinic traditions with a primeval serpent opposing creation, and possibly a serpent-like manifestation of Satan. Yet Smick is quoted: “To Job, a strict monotheist, this was simply vivid imagery.”

The **King James Version** reads “raise up their mourning” instead of “rouse Leviathan,” reflecting a different textual tradition.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/3.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-3/

---

### v.9 — “May its morning stars grow dark; may it wait in vain for daylight; may it not see the breaking of dawn.”

**Traditional reading:** “Morning stars” refers to the stars visible in the morning or evening twilight. Ellicott notes the beautiful Hebrew idiom “the eyelids of the dawn” for the first glimmer of daylight—the dawn opening its eyes. The night is personified as looking eagerly for light that never comes. The Pulpit Commentary calls it a personification of the night “consciously waiting in hope of the appearance of morning, but continually disappointed.”

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.10 — “For that night did not shut the doors of the womb to hide the sorrow from my eyes.”

**Traditional reading:** The night is imagined as having the power to close wombs. Job blames the night for failing to prevent his birth and thereby failing to hide sorrow from his eyes. Gill explains that by speaking of “the doors of my mother’s womb” (literally “my womb”), Job deliberately avoids naming God directly as the one who opens and closes the womb—trying not to complain directly against God. The Pulpit Commentary calls this “a stretch of imagination.”

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/job/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.11 — “Why did I not perish at birth; why did I not die as I came from the womb?”

**Traditional reading:** Having wished his birth-day obliterated, Job now asks why he did not at least die at birth. The Pulpit Commentary notes this reflects an ancient pessimism: the Greek poet Sophocles wrote, “Not to be born is best of all; once born, next best by far to go back whence one came as speedily as possible.” Jeremiah echoes this in Jeremiah 20:17. Guzik (Enduring Word) notes this is poetic exaggeration—Job powerfully communicates that death feels better than his present misery. Yet as Poole observes, Job never attempted suicide; he “was contented to wait all the days of his appointed time, till his change came” (Job 14:14).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-3/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.12 — “Why were there knees to receive me, and breasts that I should be nursed?”

**Traditional reading:** The “knees” are the mother’s or father’s knees, on which a newborn was placed as an act of acknowledgment and reception. Ellicott says the sense is: “Why was I nursed with care instead of being allowed to fall to the ground and be killed?” The Pulpit Commentary adds that some ancient cultures selectively raised only certain children; Job wishes he had been exposed and left to perish.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.13 — “For now I would be lying down in peace; I would be asleep and at rest”

**Traditional reading:** Job imagines death as sleep and rest. This is where **tradition differences begin to emerge**:

- **Enduring Word (Guzik, Pentecostal/charismatic):** Says Job’s view of the afterlife is “incomplete and partly wrong”—he seems to believe in something like “soul sleep,” i.e., the dead lie unconscious in the grave awaiting resurrection. Guzik says this is corrected by 2 Corinthians 5:6–8 (to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord) and Philippians 1:21, and that the OT understanding of immortality was “at best cloudy.”
- **John MacArthur (GTY, Baptist):** While MacArthur does not directly comment on v.13 in the available material, he uses Job 3:16–17 to argue that infants who die enter “rest,” not torment—affirming conscious rest after death for the innocent, not soul sleep.
- **Reformed/Presbyterian** sources were not accessible in this search for v.13 specifically.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-3/
- https://www.gty.org/sermons/80-242/the-salvation-of-babies-who-die-part-1

---

### v.14 — “with kings and counselors of the earth, who built for themselves cities now in ruins”

**Traditional reading:** Job envisions being in the grave alongside the great of the earth. Ellicott interprets “desolate places” (KJV) as “gorgeous tombs and splendid sepulchres, which, being tenanted only by the dead, are desolate”—possibly alluding to the Pyramids. The Pulpit Commentary sees three possible meanings: (a) restorers of ruined cities; (b) builders of structures that afterward became ruined; or (c) builders of desolate, dreary piles like pyramids and rock-tombs. Death levels all social distinctions—kings and nobles lie in the grave alongside everyone else.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.15 — “or with princes who had gold, who filled their houses with silver.”

**Traditional reading:** The Pulpit Commentary gives two possible senses: either simply “princes who were rich in life,” or princes who had gold and silver buried with them in their tombs. The latter reflects ancient Near Eastern burial customs (Egyptian, Phoenician, Scythian tombs filled with treasure). If so, “houses” means their tombs, which Egyptians called their “eternal abodes.”

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.16 — “Or why was I not hidden like a stillborn child, like an infant who never sees daylight?”

**Traditional reading:** Job wishes he had been stillborn—never seeing the light of life, and thus never experiencing suffering. Ellicott simply notes this as another condition that would have relieved him from suffering. 

**Tradition note:** John MacArthur (GTY, Baptist) cites vv.16–17 to support the view that infants who die enter immediately into “rest.” He says: “Job understood that dying as an infant would bring one to rest and one would escape the pain of suffering. He certainly didn’t believe that infants that die go to hell and some eternal torment but rather had the confidence that they entered into rest.” This is a distinctively Baptist (and broadly evangelical) reading that uses this passage in the debate over the eternal destiny of those dying in infancy.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/3.htm
- https://www.gty.org/sermons/80-242/the-salvation-of-babies-who-die-part-1

---

### v.17 — “There the wicked cease from raging, and there the weary find rest.”

**Traditional reading:** “There” is the grave (Sheol). The Pulpit Commentary explains: the wicked are like the troubled sea (Isaiah 57:20), perpetually restless and causing trouble; only in the grave do they cease. Guzik (Enduring Word) says Job was *wrong* in this view of the afterlife—the wicked do not “cease from troubling” in the world beyond; their trouble only increases. But Guzik acknowledges that Job “was not aiming for theological certainty … he poured out the agony of his soul.” Poole is cited: “Job meddles not here with their eternal state after death … but only speaks of their freedom from worldly troubles.”

**Baptist (GTY/MacArthur):** Uses vv.16–17 as evidence that death brings rest—particularly for infants.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-3/
- https://www.gty.org/sermons/80-242/the-salvation-of-babies-who-die-part-1

---

### v.18 — “The captives enjoy their ease; they do not hear the voice of the oppressor.”

**Traditional reading:** The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott note that “oppressor” (or “taskmaster”) is the same word used of the Egyptian slave-drivers in Exodus 3:7 and 5:6. Some commentators see a possible allusion to the Exodus story. In death, the prisoner/slave is freed from the voice of the one who drove him.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.19 — “Both small and great are there, and the slave is freed from his master.”

**Traditional reading:** Death is the great equalizer: all social ranks are leveled in the grave. The Pulpit Commentary quotes Horace: “Omnes eodem cogimur” (“We are all driven to the same place”). The slave (Hebrew *eved*) is free from his master—this is the only liberation Job can envision at this point.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.20 — “Why is light given to the miserable, and life to the bitter of soul?”

**Traditional reading:** Job now shifts from wishing he had died to questioning why God prolongs the lives of the miserable. Ellicott notes the connection between “light” and “life” that runs through Scripture (Psalm 36:9; John 1:4). Job asks: if life is a gift, why is it given to those who find it only agony? The Pulpit Commentary says this is captious questioning, answered in principle by Zophar later in Job 11:7–8 (“Can you by searching find out God?”).

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.21 — “who long for death that does not come, and search for it like hidden treasure”

**Traditional reading:** The imagery is of treasure-hunters who dig avidly. The Pulpit Commentary explains that because of the instability of Eastern governments, treasures were often hidden, and treasure-seeking became a profession pursued with great eagerness—so too these sufferers eagerly seek death. Yet Guzik notes Job does not commit suicide or even seriously contemplate it—this is the outpouring of an agonized but trusting heart.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-3/

---

### v.22 — “who rejoice and greatly exult when they can find the grave?”

**Traditional reading:** The Hebrew conveys rejoicing “to exultation” or even “to dancing.” The Pulpit Commentary calls this “morbid and unreal,” noting that “of sane men it may be doubted whether one in a thousand, however miserable, really wishes to die.” Yet the Bible records this as Job’s honest cry.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html

---

### v.23 — “Why is life given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?”

**Traditional reading:** This verse contains a bitter echo of Job 1:10, where Satan complained that God had “hedged” Job about protectively. Now Job experiences that hedge as a prison wall. Ellicott explicitly notes the same expression used in the opposite sense. Guzik (Enduring Word) says: “Job’s trouble did not come because he had lost faith in God. He felt and feared that God had lost faith in him.” The “hidden way” means Job can see no purpose or direction for his life. Andersen is quoted: “His concern from beginning to end is God; not his wealth or his health, but his life with God. It is because he seems to have lost God that he is in such torment.”

**Reformed/Baptist (Piper, Desiring God):** John Piper says in Job 3, “Job can’t see any reason for this. It’s dragging on. And he says, ‘Look, if it’s like this, if this is the way life is going to be, there was no reason for me to be born except to be tormented.’” Piper presents this as the explosion of pent-up frustration yet notes that Job’s faith wavers but does not give up.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-3/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/3.htm
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/holding-on-to-your-faith-in-the-midst-of-suffering-job-part-2

---

### v.24 — “I sigh when food is put before me, and my groans pour out like water.”

**Traditional reading:** The Pulpit Commentary translates “roarings” (for “groans”)—a word used primarily of a lion’s roar (Zechariah 11:3; Amos 3:8), indicating loud, uncontrollable cries of pain. They pour out “like water”—freely, copiously, without restraint. Guzik says: “We sense the great emotion in Job’s speech. He was not a stoic … such an emotionless Christian life is never presented to us as a Biblical ideal.”

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-3/

---

### v.25 — “For the thing I feared has overtaken me, and what I dreaded has befallen me.”

**Traditional reading:** **Two distinct interpretations** among the commentators:

1. **Job had always feared calamity, even in prosperity:** Ellicott says it means Job “had always had in remembrance the uncertainty and instability of earthly things, and yet he had been overtaken by a calamity that mocked his carefulness and exceeded his apprehensions.” Clarke (quoted in Guzik) says: “While I was in prosperity I thought adversity might come, and I had a dread of it. I feared the loss of my family and my property … I am not stripped of my all as a punishment for my self-confidence.” This connects to Job 1:5, where Job made offerings just in case his children sinned.

2. **Job’s present fears are constantly being realized:** The Pulpit Commentary interprets this as: now that he is in adversity, he is beset with fears, and all his presentiments of evil are immediately accomplished—i.e., it is not a reference to fears in his prosperous past but fears in his current misery.

Guzik and Trapp take the first view; the Pulpit Commentary takes the second. The Grant’s Commentary (Brethren) also takes the first: “He had not been feeling secure and confident of continuing in constant prosperity. He greatly feared that he might be reduced as now he found himself.”

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/3.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-3/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-3.html

---

### v.26 — “I am not at ease or quiet; I have no rest, for trouble has come.”

**Traditional reading:** Job’s speech ends with four hammer-blows: no ease, no quiet, no rest—only trouble. The Pulpit Commentary notes an alternative translation: “I slackened not, neither was I quiet, neither took I rest; yet trouble came”—meaning Job was not lax in his piety, yet calamity came anyway, making the conclusion more pointed. Guzik (Enduring Word) uses this verse to highlight that “even a great man of faith can fall into great depression and despair,” and quotes Charles Spurgeon’s own testimony of a season of weeping and low spirits. Guzik also quotes G. Campbell Morgan: “Such outpouring is a far more healthy thing for the soul than dark and silent brooding.”

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-3.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-3/

## Tradition-Specific Distinctives (Where Found)

### Baptist

- **John Gill (older Baptist):** Emphasises that Job did not curse God, his friends, or himself—only his day. Defends Job against Jewish writers who claimed he denied providence. Notes Job’s weakness but insists on his perseverance (James 5:11).
- **John MacArthur (GTY, dispensational Baptist):** Uses Job 3:16–17 to argue that infants who die enter “rest,” not condemnation. This is a distinctive Baptist contribution to the “age of accountability” / infant salvation debate.
- **John Piper (Desiring God, Reformed Baptist):** Sees Job 3 as the “explosion of Job’s pent-up frustration with God’s drawing out this suffering.” Emphasises that Job’s faith wavers but does not give up. The friends lose pastoral sensitivity by answering anguish with rigid theology.

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word – David Guzik)

- Emphasises that Job’s raw emotional honesty is not a failure of faith but a biblical reality.
- Says Job’s understanding of the afterlife (soul sleep in vv.13–19) was incomplete and later clarified by the NT.
- Reads Leviathan as possibly a “serpent-like manifestation of Satan,” connecting to Genesis 3 and Revelation 12–13.
- Strong pastoral application: depression and honest lament are healthier than stoic silence.

### Brethren / Plymouth Brethren (Grant’s Commentary)

- Emphasises that Job “was moved by his anguish, not by faith”—his wishes are impossible and show weak faith. Yet Grant notes Job never considers suicide.
- Takes the view that v.25 means Job had always feared losing his prosperity, and God allowed the dreaded thing to teach him that His grace is sufficient.

### Anglican / Older Protestant (Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary)

- Ellicott sees the chapter as the *original* that Jeremiah 20:14–18 later quoted.
- Both give careful attention to the Hebrew text and poetic devices.
- The Pulpit Commentary is notably more reserved about Job’s language, calling some of it “morbid and unreal” and “captious questioning.”

### Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan, Catholic, Orthodox

I was unable to reach LCMS, 1517.org, Wesley/Seedbed, New Advent/Catholic.com, or OCA.org pages for Job 3 within the search and fetch limits. These sources would be needed to identify distinctive readings from those traditions. A typical Lutheran reading would likely emphasise Law/Gospel dialectic (Job’s despair under the Law); a Wesleyan reading might emphasise Job’s honesty in lament as consonant with holiness (not stoic denial); Catholic commentaries (e.g., Haydock) would likely interact with the Vulgate and note the Church’s teaching on the afterlife to correct Job’s limited Sheol-view.

---

## Summary of Cross-Tradition Tensions in Job 3

| Issue | View A | View B |
|-------|--------|--------|
| **Afterlife in vv.13–19** | Soul sleep / limited OT view (Guzik, Pentecostal) | Poetic description of Sheol, not doctrinal (Pulpit, Ellicott); MacArthur uses it for infant rest |
| **Leviathan (v.8)** | Mythological chaos-dragon / possible Satanic figure (Guzik) | Crocodile / poetic imagery for reckless persons (Ellicott); Sorcerers’ power (Pulpit) |
| **“Thing I feared” (v.25)** | Job had always feared calamity in his prosperity (Ellicott, Clarke, Grant) | Job’s present fears are continuously realized (Pulpit) |
| **Job’s moral state** | Weakness of faith, later repented of (Gill, Grant) | Honest lament, not sin per se; healthier than stoicism (Guzik, Morgan) |
